cues: Welcome to Build a Game with Claude — the complete visual guide.
Prepared by Sara Salem.
In this video, you'll discover every type of game you can build with Claude, and learn how to build your own game — step by step, from the first idea to a finished game you can share with the world.
Let's start with a simple comparison.
Building a game alone usually means months of learning to code, searching for fixes, drawing art, and getting stuck on bugs.
With Claude, it's different. You describe your idea in plain words, and Claude writes the code, creates the graphics and sounds, and fixes bugs — in minutes, while you make the creative decisions.
In short: alone, a game takes months. With Claude, your first playable game takes minutes.
So, what can Claude do for your game?
Claude can turn a simple idea into a real, working game — right inside the chat.
It helps you design the game — the goal, the rules, the controls, and the levels.
It writes the code — the game loop, the movement, the collisions, and the score.
And it adds art, sound, and testing — so your game looks good, sounds good, and works well.
At its core, building a game with Claude works in a loop.
First, you describe — what you want to build, or what you want to change.
Then Claude generates the game — the code, the graphics, and the logic.
Next, you play it — and see how it feels.
And then you improve it — asking for new features and fixes. Then you repeat, until your game is fun.
Now, let's look at all the types of games you can build with Claude.
Puzzle games. Like sliding tiles, match-three, or number puzzles that make players think.
Arcade games. Classic action — like snake, breakout, or a space shooter with fast reflexes.
Platformers. A character that runs and jumps across platforms, collecting coins and avoiding enemies.
Quiz and trivia games. Questions, timers, and scores — great for learning and for classrooms.
Strategy and board games. Like tic-tac-toe, chess, or card games, with a computer opponent.
And 3D games. Using libraries like Three dot js, Claude can build simple 3D worlds that run in the browser.
There are four main ways to build a game with Claude.
Artifacts. Claude builds the game right in the chat, and you can play it instantly — no setup needed.
Claude Code. For bigger games, Claude Code works with all the files in your project on your computer.
Game libraries. Claude can use tools like Phaser for 2D games, or Three dot js for 3D games.
And the Claude API. You can even add Claude inside your game — to power smart characters and dialogue.
Now let's build a real game, step by step. Step one: start your game.
Open Claude, and start a new chat.
Describe your game in one clear sentence — here, a space shooter called Star Defender.
Ask for a single HTML file, with a canvas — so it runs in any browser.
Then play it instantly, right in the chat, as an artifact.
Step two: write a game design brief.
Start with the concept — the name, the genre, and the goal of the game.
Then define the controls — which keys move the player, and which key shoots.
Write the rules — how players score points, and how they lose lives.
And describe the style — the colors, the look, and the mood. A clear brief gives you a much better first version.
Step three: understand the game loop. Every game has three layers.
Layer one is input — reading the keyboard, the mouse, or touch on mobile.
Layer two is update — moving the player and enemies, checking collisions, and updating the score.
Layer three is render — drawing everything on the screen, again and again.
This loop runs about sixty times every second — that's what makes the game feel smooth and alive.
Step four: add the game mechanics.
Here's our next request: add enemies, power-ups, and a score.
First, the player — a ship that moves smoothly and shoots.
Then enemies — that appear in waves, and move in patterns.
Next, collisions — so lasers destroy enemies, and enemies damage the player.
Then the score, and finally levels — each one a little faster and harder than the last.
Step five: balance the difficulty.
Ask Claude to make the game easy to start, but harder as players improve.
Watch how the difficulty rises level by level. In this example, it climbs smoothly — with no sudden jumps that frustrate players.
Six levels, more enemies in every wave, and ten playtests to get the balance right.
The golden rule: easy to learn, hard to master.
Step six: add art and sound.
Graphics. Claude can draw the ship, the enemies, and the backgrounds with code — no image files needed.
Animations. Particles, explosions, and glowing effects make every action feel exciting.
Sound effects. With the Web Audio API, Claude can create laser sounds and explosions from code.
And menus and screens. A start menu, a pause screen, and a game over screen with a play again button.
Step seven: test and fix.
Play your game, and look for anything that feels wrong.
Then tell Claude exactly what happened — for example, the ship can fly off the screen.
Claude finds the problem, fixes the code, and can even add small improvements — like a pause key.
Then play again. Testing and fixing in small rounds is the fastest way to a great game.
Step eight: polish your game.
Add a high score — saved in the browser, so players can try to beat their best.
Add mobile controls — touch buttons, so the game works on phones and tablets.
Add bosses and new levels — big challenges that keep players coming back.
And add options — like sound on and off, and difficulty settings, so everyone can enjoy it.
Step nine: share your game with the world.
Publish your artifact and share the link. Send it to friends. And let others remix it to make their own version.
Download the HTML file. Host it on GitHub Pages. Or publish it on game sites like itch dot io.
Collect feedback from players, and keep updating your game. Every version can be better than the last.
Here are six best practices for building games with Claude.
One: start small — build a simple, playable version first.
Two: write a clear brief — the goal, the controls, the rules, and the style.
Three: add one feature at a time, and test after each change.
Four: describe bugs exactly — what you did, what happened, and what you expected.
Five: playtest with real players, and listen to their feedback.
And six: keep it fun — fun always comes before features.
So, building a game with Claude in one line: imagine, build, play. You bring the ideas — Claude helps you turn them into real games.
From a simple puzzle to a 3D world, your next game is just one prompt away.
Thank you for watching this complete guide to building a game with Claude.
